# Results — Study 364 (FX Carry Trade)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The **FX carry trade** — borrow
low-yield currencies, hold high-yield ones, pocket the rate differential — tested on a
**yfinance G10 FX tape** with a **transparent carry proxy**. True deposit-rate differentials
are not bundled on yfinance, so carry is a fixed per-currency constant (a long-run average
annualised short-rate gap vs USD), named a proxy throughout. We build the long-high /
short-low dollar-neutral basket, then measure not only its mean and Sharpe but the **shape**
of the distribution — skew, worst month, drawdown, and the crash-conditional split — because
the whole question is whether the premium is a free lunch or a sold-insurance payoff.
Offline & deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily FX spot — 9 G10 pairs vs USD (public, no key), normalised to USD-per-foreign |
| As-of | 2026-06-19 (pull); window 2004-01-01 → 2026-06-19 |
| Span | **5,847** trading days; **269** month-end observations; **22.5** years |
| Carry | fixed per-currency annualised short-rate-diff vs USD; **PROXY** for true deposit rates |
| Basket | rank by carry; **long top-3** (AUD, NZD, NOK) / **short bottom-3** (EUR, JPY, CHF), dollar-neutral, monthly |
| Entry / costs | one-month hold; 2 bps one-way on the gross book + borrow on the short leg (default 50 bps/yr) |

> **Proxy caveat (named on the Signal axis).** Attaching a *constant* carry to each currency
> ignores the time-variation in rate differentials (the carry was wide pre-2008 and compressed
> in the zero-rate decade). The fixed proxy preserves the **cross-sectional ordering**
> (commodity high-yielders long, JPY/CHF funding currencies short) that defines the trade, and
> the verdict hinges on the basket's *shape* (skew, crash) — which a constant carry cannot
> manufacture — not on the exact carry levels. A time-varying carry would lower the mean
> further in the zero-rate years without removing the crash tail.

## The signal — a positive premium, but a low Sharpe and a fat left tail

The dollar-neutral carry basket (long AUD/NZD/NOK, short EUR/JPY/CHF), monthly, 2004→2026:

| metric | value | reading |
|---|--:|---|
| annualised mean (gross) | **+1.97%** | UIP fails — carry is positive, as the lore says |
| annualised Sharpe (gross) | **0.25** | thin; nowhere near the "free lunch" Sharpe of legend |
| HAC *t* of the mean | **1.14** | **fails the t ≥ 2 bar** — indistinguishable from zero |
| skewness | **−0.75** | the tell: the distribution is **left-skewed** |
| worst single month | **−11.73%** | a year-and-a-half of carry wiped out in one month |
| max drawdown | **−35.3%** | the carry crash, drawn to scale |

The mean is positive but small and **statistically insignificant** on this tape (HAC
*t* = 1.14). More importantly, the distribution is **negatively skewed (−0.75)**: the carry
grinds up in calm months and collapses in risk-off ones. That is the signature of a **sold
insurance policy**, not of an arbitrage.

## The crash skew — where the "free lunch" is paid back

Split the 269 months into the calmest 90% and the worst 10% (27 months):

| bucket | annualised mean | what it is |
|---|--:|---|
| calm months (best 90%) | **+8.0%/yr** | the carry "grind" — looks like easy money |
| risk-off months (worst 10%) | **−52.2%/yr** | the carry crash — the bill comes due |

The worst-decile months alone give back **2.66×** the basket's entire cumulative gain. The
calendar names them for you — the six worst months are **Oct 2008** (−11.7%, GFC), **Mar 2020**
(−8.0%, COVID), **Jan 2015** (−5.9%, the SNB CHF de-peg), **Dec 2008**, **Nov 2007**, **Sep 2008**.
Carry doesn't lose money at random; it loses money *exactly* when every other risky asset does,
which is why it cannot be a free lunch: you are being paid a premium to bear crash risk.

## Costs — a borrow drag the thin premium can't absorb

| borrow on the short leg | net mean | net Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps/yr | +1.49% | 0.19 |
| 25 bps/yr | +1.24% | 0.16 |
| **50 bps/yr** (default) | **+0.99%** | **0.12** |
| 100 bps/yr | +0.49% | 0.06 |

The carry book is short funding currencies, so it pays **borrow** every month it is on. At a
realistic 50 bps/yr the net premium is **+0.99%/yr** at a **net Sharpe of 0.12** — half the
already-thin gross — and at 100 bps it is essentially gone. The crash tail, of course, is
unchanged: you keep the −35% drawdown and surrender most of the grind to costs.

## Robustness — the shape is the same at every basket width

| k (currencies per leg) | ann. mean | Sharpe | HAC *t* | skew | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | +4.95% | 0.37 | 1.74 | −0.72 | −65.6% |
| 2 | +2.86% | 0.28 | 1.33 | −0.81 | −47.0% |
| **3** (headline) | **+1.97%** | **0.25** | **1.14** | **−0.75** | **−35.3%** |
| 4 | +1.44% | 0.24 | 1.11 | −0.82 | −29.2% |

Concentrating into the single highest/lowest yielder (k=1) raises the mean and Sharpe — and
the drawdown to **−66%**, with the same negative skew. There is no width at which the HAC *t*
clears 2; tighter baskets just trade more mean for more crash. The negative skew is a constant
of the trade, not a parameter artefact.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine recovers premium *and* crash, and stays honest

A deterministic FX panel (240 months, 8 currencies, seed 364) with a *known* carry premium
and a *known* fat-tailed crash injected by construction:

| configuration | ann. mean | Sharpe | HAC *t* | skew | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **null** (no carry, no crash) | −1.82% | −0.19 | **−0.79** | +0.44 | −70.4% |
| carry only (premium, no crash) | +6.82% | +0.71 | **+2.95** | −0.44 | −21.5% |
| carry + crash skew | −2.55% | −0.16 | −0.77 | **−3.99** | −77.9% |
| big planted edge + crash | +11.74% | +0.75 | **+3.56** | −3.99 | −43.5% |

The control proves three things at once. **(1)** With no planted carry the test does **not**
cross t = 2 (HAC *t* = −0.79) — the engine cannot manufacture significance from noise. **(2)**
A planted carry premium lights up (t = 2.95), and a large planted excess lights up harder
(t = 3.56) — the machinery banks a real edge when one exists. **(3)** Switching on the crash
knob drives skew to **−3.99** and turns the premium *negative* — the carry-crash mechanism is
exactly what the real tape shows in miniature, on data where we know the truth.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The carry premium is positive (**+1.97%/yr**) — UIP genuinely fails, as
  the literature says — but on this 22-year G10 tape it is small and **fails the t ≥ 2 bar**
  (HAC *t* = 1.14), and it carries a **−0.75 skew** with a **−35% drawdown**. Decades of
  published support + a positive-but-insignificant mean ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL. (The carry proxy
  is fixed, which only *flatters* the mean in the zero-rate years.)
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Net of a realistic borrow the premium is **+0.99%/yr at Sharpe
  0.12**, and it comes attached to a fat left tail that wipes out years of grind in a single
  risk-off month (worst month −11.7%, max DD −35%). A thin, crash-prone, costs-sensitive edge
  is survivable on paper but is **not a NAV-scale, set-and-forget allocation**.
- **Free lunch? — BUSTED.** The carry trade is **not** free money: in calm months it earns
  +8%/yr, in the worst decile it loses −52%/yr, and the tail gives back 2.66× the cumulative
  gain. The premium is **compensation for selling crash insurance** — exactly when you most
  need your portfolio, the carry is what blows up. High Sharpe, deeply negative skew: a sold
  insurance policy in a trench coat.
